*An in-class activity. There is nothing to turn in, and most of these questions
have more than one defensible answer -- the point is the case you make for
yours.*

**The idea.** The assignment will have you read scatterplots and compute
correlations. This activity starts from the opposite end: identical correlations
that mean entirely different things, and what you would actually *do* about each
one.

**Format.** About 25 minutes · pairs · one laptop per pair.

## 1. One number, four datasets (8 minutes)

Anscombe's quartet, from the lecture: four datasets, all with $r = .816$, the
same means, and the same regression line.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

anscombe_long <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c(".value", "set"),
               names_pattern = "(.)(.)")

anscombe_long |> group_by(set) |> summarize(r = cor(x, y))

ggplot(anscombe_long, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~set)
```
:::


A collaborator hands you each of these four and asks "how strongly are these
related?" Write the *action* you would take in each case -- not the
interpretation, the next thing you would do.

- For which of the four is $r = .816$ an honest summary?
- One of them has a correlation driven almost entirely by a single point. What
  would you do, and what would you have to report either way?
- One of them is a perfect deterministic relationship that $r$ badly
  understates. What would you report instead?
- Nothing in the four numbers distinguishes these situations. What does that
  imply about a paper that reports a correlation matrix and no plots?

## 2. Same $r$, different consequence (8 minutes)

All four studies below report $r = .30$, $p < .05$. Decide what you would do
next in each case, and say where the difference in your reaction comes from --
because it is not coming from the number.

> **A.** A 15-year study of 40,000 people finds $r = .30$ between childhood
> adversity and adult depression.

> **B.** An undergraduate project with $n = 45$ finds $r = .30$ between hours of
> sleep and exam score.

> **C.** $r = .30$ between a new 4-item screening tool and a full clinical
> diagnosis.

> **D.** $r = .30$ between two administrations of the same questionnaire, a week
> apart.

- Two of these are good results and two are bad ones. Which, and why?
- For B, what is the confidence interval around .30 roughly going to look like?
  What is the honest one-sentence summary of that study?
- What does this tell you about reporting a correlation without an interval?

## 3. The third variable game (6 minutes)

Take a real correlation from your own area -- one you believe.

- Your partner's job is to propose three third variables that could produce it
  without any direct relationship existing.
- Then swap. Then, for each proposal, say what data you would need to rule it
  out.
- Finally: which of the proposals could be ruled out by *measuring* something,
  and which could only be ruled out by *designing* something differently?

## 4. Whole class (3 minutes)

- One sentence: what does $r^2$ add that $r$ does not, and what does it lose?

{{< dstart summary="If you were not in class" >}}

Anscombe's four: set 1 is a genuine linear relationship and $r = .816$ describes
it honestly. Set 2 is a clean curve, and the right action is to fit the curve,
not to report the correlation. Set 3 is a perfect straight line plus one
outlier, and the action is to find out what happened with that observation
before doing anything else -- the correlation without it is essentially 1. Set 4
is a vertical stack of points at one $x$ value plus a single distant point; the
correlation is being computed from what is effectively two locations, and there
is no relationship to report at all.

The lesson is not "distrust correlations" -- it is that a correlation answers one
narrow question, how much of the pattern is a straight line, and answers it well.
A correlation matrix with no plots is not wrong, it is simply insufficient
evidence that any of its entries mean what they appear to.

On the four studies: A and D are the informative ones and C and B are the
problems. $r = .30$ is a respectable effect for a life-course risk factor
(study A, and with $n = 40{,}000$ it is precisely estimated). It is a poor
screening tool (C) -- you would misclassify constantly. It is a *disastrous*
test-retest reliability (D): the questionnaire is mostly measuring noise, and
every effect you estimate with it will be attenuated, which is the subject of
Chapter 13. Study B's interval runs roughly from .01 to .55, so the honest
summary is "somewhere between nothing and a lot," and reporting ".30,
significant" without that interval is the misleading part.

On third variables: the useful distinction at the end is that some confounds can
be measured and adjusted for, and others cannot be separated from your predictor
by any amount of measurement -- those need randomization or a different design.
Recognizing which kind you are facing early is worth more than any analysis
choice later.
